label: Topshelf Records
description: Ratboys' debut LP: unhurried, twang-flecked indie rock built around Julia Steiner's plainspoken voice and long, patient song structures. A quieter, more folk-adjacent record than the band's later output, closer to their alt-country roots.
lineage: Grew out of Steiner and Sagan's college-band beginnings at Notre Dame; set the twangy-indie template the band expanded on GN and Printer's Devil.

label: Topshelf Records
description: Second Ratboys LP: warm, unhurried indie rock with country phrasing and Steiner's conversational storytelling. Quieter and more spacious than the band's later, harder-rocking records.
lineage: Bridges the band's early alt-country leanings with the bigger, distorted guitar sound they'd bring on Printer's Devil.

label: Topshelf Records
description: Ratboys' loudest, most confident record to that point: bigger choruses and full-band muscle layered over the same plainspoken, twang-inflected songwriting. It suits listeners who like their indie rock warm, hooky and a little country.
lineage: Marks the move from their earlier folk-adjacent sound toward the anthemic guitar rock of The Window and Singin' to an Empty Chair.

label: Topshelf Records
description: A tenth-anniversary record revisiting older songs with the full band, playing them at their most direct and hooky. It sits between the loose twang of GN and the polish of The Window.
lineage: A victory-lap record marking Ratboys' first decade before their Chris Walla-produced pivot.

label: Topshelf Records
description: Chris Walla-produced fifth LP blending alt-rock, country twang and a little emo, the fullest version of Ratboys' patient songwriting. Highlights include the elegiac 'Black Earth, WI' and the wired 'Morning Zoo'.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with Wednesday and MJ Lenderman in the current wave of twangy Midwest/Southern indie rock.

label: New West Records
description: Ratboys' latest LP: massive-sounding, anthemic indie rock with lilting twang and frantic shredding. Julia Steiner's plainspoken voice holds the center while the guitars push the songs toward big, cathartic endings.
lineage: Continues the arc from AOID's quiet twang through The Window's alt-rock/country/emo blend.

label: 12XU
description: Florry's turn toward Gram Parsons-style Cosmic American Music: pedal steel, honky-tonk piano and Neil Young-indebted guitar wrapped around Francie Medosch's songwriting. It is warm, loose and hopeful, made for fans of ragged '70s country-rock.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Parsons' Cosmic American Music and Neil Young; precedes the caustic barroom twang of The Holey Bible.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A short, ramshackle punk-country EP that sounds built for beers in a small, sticky room. It works as a loose bridge between Big Fall and the fuller-band Holey Bible, with rough guitars and Medosch's warbling voice up front.
lineage: Part of the same Dear Life Records-era run of scrappy, caustic Philly country as The Holey Bible.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Florry's Dear Life Records debut proper: raucous, barroom-ready country-rock with a half-broken pedal steel, fiddle and a full band behind Francie Medosch's caustic, warble-voiced songwriting. It sits somewhere between the Replacements and Drive-By Truckers, built for loud rooms and cold beer.
lineage: A Dear Life Records release that sounds of a piece with the indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Florry's second full-band album: rambunctious barroom twang with Rolling Thunder-style energy alongside quieter, more understated songs. Fiddle, pedal steel and loose group vocals keep it feeling like a party that occasionally sobers up.
lineage: Continues the Dear Life Records run of The Holey Bible; sounds close to the Asheville indie-twang of MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

label: Loose Music
description: Debut LP from Norwich's Brown Horse: stark, road-worn alt-country with twangy guitars and weary, shared vocals. It establishes the band's slow-burning songwriting before the fuller sound of All the Right Weaknesses.
lineage: A UK band that sounds steeped in the American alt-country/Crazy Horse tradition, close in spirit to Wednesday and Greg Freeman.

label: Loose Music
description: Brown Horse's second LP: soaring guitars, blissful pedal steel and earnest vocals melding slacker rock, folk and alt-country. It sits near Greg Freeman, Wednesday and Neil Young in feel, loud but tender.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Lucinda Williams, Jason Molina and Silver Jews; part of the UK's small but active indie-twang scene.

label: Fluff and Gravy Records
description: Brown Horse's third LP: brooding, twangy guitar rock with fuzzy riffs, pedal steel and country-rock arrangements. It keeps the band's weary vocals and slow-building dynamics but leans heavier than before.
lineage: Continues the band's alt-country arc from Reservoir and All the Right Weaknesses.

note: Debut LP mentioned in Florry's Big Fall Bandcamp bio (Sister Polygon, 2018); no tracklist or dedicated page found to confirm key tracks.

label: Big Legal Mess Records
description: Thomas Dollbaum's debut LP: dark rural storytelling sung in a rangy baritone, with Southern gothic detail and spare, dusty arrangements. It is for listeners who like their country songs literary, slow and haunted.
lineage: Sounds rooted in the alt-country storytelling lineage of Townes Van Zandt and Jason Molina.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A short EP of hushed, tragic story-songs set on Florida backroads. It works as a brief bridge between Wellswood and Birds of Paradise, with Dollbaum's baritone close to the mic over quiet guitar.
lineage: Brings Dollbaum's alt-country storytelling into the Dear Life Records fold alongside Florry.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Dollbaum's second LP: roaring Americana shading into tender folk, sung in a rangy, raspy baritone with strong harmonies. It plays like a goodbye letter to lost loved ones, set among Florida's pine flatwoods.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Townes Van Zandt and Jason Molina while stepping out of their shadow.

label: Self-released
description: An early self-released Spencer Radcliffe LP of sparse, home-recorded songs. Its hushed vocals and simple guitar sketches anticipate the twangier, more rock-oriented turn of his later solo work.
lineage: An early entry in Radcliffe's long solo catalogue that eventually feeds into the twangier Ohio Vision.
borderline_note: Sound not directly confirmed as twang/country; included as completion of an artist mapped to C1, sequenced before his rockier records.

label: Run For Cover Records
description: Radcliffe's first Run For Cover full-length: patchwork indie pop and lo-fi textures held together by his flat, equivocal voice. It is homemade and a little strange, for listeners who like bedroom pop with rough edges.
lineage: Sounds part of the same Run for Cover/Topshelf-adjacent 2010s indie underground as Ratboys.

label: Orindal Records
description: Radcliffe's twangy return: fuzzy, hypnotic rock and rambling jams chronicling a return home to Ohio. It is propulsive and relaxed by turns, Midwest indie rock with a country lean.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the current wave of Midwest indie-twang alongside Ratboys and i26connector.

label: Self-released
description: An Asheville project's debut, self-tagged 'Emo Southern Rock': wailing pedal steel and booming riffs under conversational lyrics. The songs swing from barroom talk to apocalyptic brooding.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday, blending twangy Southern rock with an emo-adjacent intensity.
borderline_note: Self-tagged 'Emo Southern Rock'; could also fit C9 (twangy emo crossover) as secondary.

label: Self-released
description: Oldstar's studio debut: raucous, meaty overdriven country rock with fiddle and outlaw phrasing, recalling Lenderman, Steve Earle, Drive-By Truckers and Being There-era Wilco. A concept record about highway wandering, bar to bar.
lineage: Sounds indebted to outlaw country and Wilco's Being There; close in spirit to young Southern indie-twang songwriters like Thomas Dollbaum and i26connector.
borderline_note: Real Bandcamp handle is oldst4r (band tags itself 'oldstar'); a different band uses the plain 'oldstar' handle.

label: Self-released
description: Zachary James's efficient, hooky home-recording project: '90s alt-rock and Pavement/Big Star-style jangle folded into twangy, deceptively simple songs. It is short, bright and replayable, for fans of warm, lo-fi guitar pop.
lineage: Part of the same Burlington scene as Greg Freeman; its songwriting sounds indebted to Judee Sill, Alex Chilton and Elliott Smith.

album: I Saw A Galloping Horse Cover No Ground
label: Anything Bagel
description: Joseph Barresi's Chico States LP: dusky, encyclopedic Americana with pedal steel and scrappy harmonies. It mixes personal minutiae with train-line and travel history, like a homemade folk archive.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Lomax-style folk documentation and cosmic Americana, close to the Northeast's alt-country underground.

label: Self-released
description: A.S. Wilson's second Convinced Friend LP: compact, forceful tracks fusing serene twang with apocalyptic indie rock. The songs reflect on home, loss and a changing coastline, moving from calm to loud without warning.
lineage: Sounds close to the Northeast slowcore/twang orbit of Horse Jumper of Love and Friendship.

album: How to Get Away with Nothing
label: Candlepin Records
description: Columbus songwriter Abel's self-lacerating, ramshackle country-jangle LP. It is loud guitar music for quiet people, with jangly guitars, clattering drums and bruised, self-deprecating lyrics.
lineage: Sounds part of the small-label DIY twang network alongside Ohio- and Midwest-based indie-country peers like Spencer Radcliffe.

label: Self-released
description: New Orleans band's 13-song LP steeped in Gulf Coast heat and road-worn twang; loose, rowdy cowpunk energy carried across tracks like the title cut and 'Swamp'.
lineage: Part of the current New Orleans indie-twang scene alongside Thomas Dollbaum, touring with Kurt Vile.

label: Self-released
description: Owen Burton's debut as Ovven: a fuzz-guitar alt-country record with loud, driving arrangements and a drawled, plainspoken voice. It suits listeners who like Crazy Horse-style guitar under country song shapes.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville-adjacent indie-twang of Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

album: Watch Me Drive Them Dogs Wild
label: Self-released
description: The Pittsburgh songwriter's breakout LP: warbling steel and outlaw-tinged guitars swelling into feedback-heavy catharsis. Her songs of loss, land and family community are sung in a clear, plain voice that the band slowly overwhelms.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville indie-twang of Florry and Wednesday.

label: Fire Talk
description: Wild Pink's most twang-coded record: driving, intense indie rock with pedal steel threading through the arrangements. Its lyrics about contemporary malaise are searing, funny and wrenching by turns.
lineage: Sounds like Wild Pink's turn toward the Core indie-twang sound; ruled into C1 as a specific stylistic pivot rather than the band's whole catalogue.
key_tracks: Round Of Applause At The End Of The World
borderline_note: Wild Pink's earlier albums (Wild Pink, Yolk in the Fur, A Billion Little Lights, ILYSM, Dulling the Horns) are straighter indie rock and are NOT included here; only Still Coming Down was ruled into C1.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Austin quartet's debut: blue-collar, plainspoken indie rock with Replacements swagger and War on Drugs-style desert-rock riffs from guitarist Jake Ames, writing about home and growing up around conservatives.
lineage: Bandleader Tyler Jordan met Jake Ames at Kerrville Folk Festival song swaps (where they also crossed paths with Buck Meek and Adrianne Lenker); Keeled Scales labelmates of Katy Kirby.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Good Looks' second LP: conversational, big-hearted indie rock with big riffs and a steady, resilient mood. Its plainspoken storytelling about working people sits over warm, twangy guitars.
lineage: Continues the band's blue-collar Austin storytelling from Bummer Year into a bigger, more electric sound.

label: Fire Talk
description: Blair Howerton's second Why Bonnie LP: twangy, expansive rock that widens the country-coded debut 90 in November into more cinematic, ambitious soundscapes. Fiddle and harmonies still anchor the quieter moments, while the louder songs swell into big, glossy guitar rock.
lineage: Follows 90 in November, whose country sound sits near Waxahatchee and Wednesday, before opening out toward Broken Social Scene/HAIM-style pop-rock.

label: Third Man Records
description: Nance's record with his full band Mowed Sound: interlocking, jammed-out guitar rock that sounds deeply indebted to Crazy Horse. Long, ragged solos and a heavy, loose rhythm section push the songs well past the three-minute mark.
lineage: Sounds like a Midwest continuation of the Crazy Horse guitar-jam trunk line that also runs through Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

album: May You Live Forever in Cowboy Heaven
label: Self-released
description: A Nashville band's ramshackle, woozy-twang record with fiddle and Built to Spill/Elephant 6-style energy. The songs are loose and wordy, with homemade production and big, sloppy singalong moments.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young and Silver Jews, sitting within the same trunk lines as the rest of the Core.

label: Self-released
description: Kevin Copeland's solo debut: punchy, twangy pop-rock and winsome folk. 'That's All Over Now' is an outright country barnstormer, while 'MONEY' leans into a bluesy stomp.
lineage: Sounds part of the Vermont/Northeast indie-folk-to-twang orbit of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.
